headline: High-risk shared-workspace pair: default filesystem overlap and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action hazards.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write files, and B explicitly shares state with other instances via the filesystem while A uses /app/storage and /tmp. That creates a default content bridge where attacker-controlled workflow or code files from A can be consumed by B as instructions. No stronger isolation is documented.
conditions: IF A writes untrusted content into shared workspace files or /app/storage
IF B ingests workspace files as prompts or instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate A and B into distinct directories
Disable automatic file ingestion in B
Add provenance labels to shared files
Review any file-based prompts before execution
requires-engineering: enforce workspace ACL isolation

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches logs, inputs, artifacts, database data, cloud storage data, messages, and notifications, while B can read workspace files and send data to configured model APIs and MCP servers. In a shared workspace, sensitive A outputs can flow into B and then out to third-party services by default configuration.
conditions: IF A stores sensitive workflow outputs in shared files
IF B forwards workspace contents to its configured model API or MCP server
mitigations: Keep sensitive A outputs out of shared folders
Use separate service accounts and API keys
Restrict B to local-only models
Redact secrets before B reads files
requires-engineering: add DLP controls on workspace egress

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have broad filesystem write, shell execution, and subprocess spawning; B also modifies git state and shares state via filesystem. In a shared workspace, concurrent writes can corrupt files or git history, and A's orchestration plus B's editor actions can race without locking. This is dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace or git repository
IF either agent writes without external locking
mitigations: Assign separate worktrees
Pause one agent during git operations
Use file locks for shared artifacts
Limit B's git writes to reviewed branches
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate workflow outputs, logs, and notifications, and B can act on files, run shells, and use MCP or browser tooling. If B treats A's outputs as authoritative, A's mistakes can cascade into code changes, commits, or external actions. The pair lacks a documented verification barrier, so the safer severity is high.
conditions: IF B uses A-produced files, logs, or notifications as ground truth
IF B performs commits, package installs, or MCP actions based on A output
mitigations: Require human review before B acts on A output
Add a verification step against source systems
Mark A outputs as untrusted by default
Disable auto-commit paths in B
requires-engineering: implement signed handoff artifacts

E_compliance.rationale: A explicitly handles database data, cloud storage data, messages, and notifications, while B handles source code and browser screenshots and can transmit data to configured model APIs. If regulated data is placed into the shared workspace, B may export it to third-party services without a documented residency or retention boundary. The profiles do not prove a specific residency mismatch, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace
IF B sends that data to a non-compliant model API or MCP server
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of B-visible files
Use compliant model endpoints only
Review retention settings for both tools
Separate logs by data class
requires-engineering: document residency and DPA boundaries
